name: Electric shaver (foil/rotary)

lead: An electric shaver cuts hair with moving blades behind a perforated foil or rotary head, so the blades do not touch the skin directly. The payoff is a clean, tidy face or body with less redness than blades, according to mostly manufacturer research.

Foil models are often described as closer-cutting, while rotary models suit some face shapes and beards better. A motor oscillates or rotates the cutters; hairs enter holes or slots and are sheared against the guard. Research on skin comfort is mostly from the cosmetic industry, including a 2016 review on reducing shaving-induced irritation.

paras: People shave dry or with a compatible wet-shave mode, using foil or rotary heads depending on their beard and face shape. Skin often needs a period to adjust to electric shaving, and results last until the hair regrows.
Irritation is possible, and case reports describe contact allergy to nickel or fragrance components in shavers. Little independent comparative research exists.

angle.text: A foil or rotary electric shaver gives a clean, tidy shave that is visible immediately, with less redness than blades according to mostly manufacturer research. Foil models are often described as closer-cutting.

lead: An electric shaver, also called an electric razor or dry shaver, is a handheld grooming device in which a motor drives oscillating or rotating blades behind a protective perforated guard, cutting facial or body hair without direct blade contact with the skin.[1] People use it to keep the face clean-shaven or evenly stubbled, which affects how neat, symmetrical and well-groomed a face looks, and many choose it because it can be used dry, quickly and with less visible irritation than blade shaving. The two main designs are foil shavers, which use a thin perforated foil over oscillating cutters, and rotary shavers, which use rotating cutting heads.[1][2]

Wikipedia notes that foil shavers can shave closer to the skin and are often preferred by professional barbers, while users tend to favour one type over the other.[2] Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, puts the closeness of foil shavers at roughly 0.05 to 0.1 mm and rotary shavers at about 0.1 mm, and describes rotary heads as better at following the contours of the jawline.[1]

The category has a century-long history, from an 1898 patent through Jacob Schick's 1930 dry shaver, the Philips rotary Philishave of 1939 and Braun's foil-and-cutter-block design, to today's wet/dry, rechargeable models with cleaning stations.[2][3][4][5] Wikipedia's article on shaving describes electric shavers as causing fewer cuts and potentially reducing razor bumps, while not necessarily cutting as closely as a blade.[6]

Electric shaving is commonly offered as an alternative to blade razors for people who find wet shaving irritating, although published sources describe skin comfort as something manufacturers have had to balance against how closely the device cuts. A 2016 review from the cosmetic science literature describes research aimed at reducing electric-shaving-induced skin irritation.[7] No randomised clinical trial comparing electric shavers with blade razors for appearance outcomes has been found.
infobox: Mains or rechargeable battery; many models are wet/dry [2]

Foil and cutter cassettes about every 12 to 18 months (Grokipedia) [1]

paras: Foil shavers pass hairs through a thin perforated foil to oscillating cutters beneath; Wikipedia notes they can shave closer to the skin and are often preferred by professional barbers. Rotary shavers use rotating blades across the head.[2] Grokipedia describes typical motor speeds of 10,000 to 14,000 cycles per minute.[1]

Grokipedia says foil models suit straight strokes on flat areas such as the cheeks, whereas rotary heads have floating discs that pivot around the jaw and neck, and that Panasonic and Braun are leading foil brands while Philips Norelco leads in rotary.[1] It also reports that one review found a Braun foil model slightly closer on short, dense stubble and a Norelco rotary more comfortable on contours and longer growth, without a controlled study behind the comparison.[1]

Early models were for dry skin only, while many modern shavers are waterproof or water-resistant and can be used in the shower.[2] Wikipedia also notes that skin often needs time to adjust to how an electric razor lifts and cuts hair, and that moisturisers designed for electric shaving exist.[2]

Grokipedia adds that foil cutters are angled at about 30 degrees, that Braun foil models add a centre trimmer to pre-cut longer hairs, and that rotary shavers use three or more floating circular heads with slotted outer rings and spinning inner cutters, turning at roughly 2,000 RPM and coping with coarser or curly growth.[1] Hybrid and trimmer-style designs combine shaving and trimming, and specialised women's, body and head (scalp) groomers use wider heads, guards or dome-shaped rotary heads.[1][2]

Wikipedia treats an electric razor and an electric trimmer as similar devices by build. Razors are made for a clean shave, while trimmers carry guide combs for shaping beard stubble to a chosen length.[2] Cordless models with charging or cleaning docks are now common, and travel shavers may use replaceable batteries.[2]

Modern models are described as running on nickel-metal-hydride or lithium-ion batteries (earlier nickel-cadmium), with 45 to 90 minutes of cordless runtime, USB-C charging and 100 to 240 V universal voltage common; some travel shavers take replaceable AA or AAA cells.[2][1] Cleaning stations from Braun and Panasonic wash and dry the head, and some lubricate the cutters.[1] Wet use is usually done with thin, clear, quick-rinsing gels, while heavy or aerosol foams can clog the heads, according to Grokipedia.[1]

Grokipedia advises rinsing after each use, brushing and oiling the cutters weekly, and replacing foil and cutter cassettes about every 12 to 18 months and rotary heads about every two years; it estimates overall lifespans of three to seven years and lists pulling and extra passes as signs of dull cutters.[1] A user on a buy-it-for-life forum reported a 16-year-old Braun Series 5 whose battery still held a charge, noting that replacement foils for that model had become hard to find.[8]

John Francis O'Rourke, a New York civil engineer, filed a US patent for an electric razor in 1898, and German engineer Johann Bruecker reportedly built the first working electric razor in 1915.[2] Grokipedia describes Jacob Schick as conceiving the dry shaver in the 1910s and receiving a 1928 patent and a 1930 patent for a design with an integrated motor.[1] Wikipedia's biography gives Schick's life as 1877 to 1937: an Iowa-born army officer who had earlier invented an injector razor (prototyped 1921, patented 1923), sold that business in 1928 to fund his electric razor, patented his electric razor in May 1930 and founded Schick Dry Shaver, Inc.[3] He is often called the father of the modern electric razor; Remington Rand began producing a razor in 1937.[2]

Alexandre Horowitz of Philips Laboratories designed one of the first rotary shavers, introduced as the Philishave in 1939.[1][2] World War II delayed its US introduction until 1948, and US sales did not take off until a two-headed model in 1951; because Philco could block use of the Philips name in the United States, Philips sold there as Norelco (North American Philips Company), a name still used alongside Philips for US shavers.[4]

Max Braun's company in Frankfurt designed its first shaver, the S 50, in 1938; the Second World War delayed its release to about 1950-51. It used an oscillating cutter block beneath a thin steel foil, the basis of the foil shaver.[5] Braun's Sixtant followed in 1962-63, Gillette took a majority stake in 1967 and full ownership by 1984, and Procter and Gamble acquired Gillette in 2005.[5] Roland Ullmann of Braun is credited with over 100 patents on dry shavers and was the first to combine rubber and metal elements.[2] Design head Dieter Rams, who led Braun's design department for nearly 30 years until 1995, is known for his Ten Principles for Good Design.[5]

Battery-powered models appeared in the late 1940s, and Remington introduced the first rechargeable model in 1960.[2] Grokipedia adds that nickel-cadmium cells spread in the 1950s and 1960s, that Panasonic patented wet/dry operation in 1985, that Philips introduced three-head rotary models in the mid-1990s, that lithium-ion batteries became common in the 2000s, and that Braun's 2015 Series 9 added an automated cleaning and maintenance centre.[1] Grokipedia reports that Braun, Philips Norelco and Panasonic lead the market, with Xiaomi and Laifen also prominent and Asia Pacific the largest region.[1]

Grokipedia states that the foil acts as a barrier that reduces friction and that foil shavers cause fewer ingrown hairs than multi-blade manual razors, while rotary heads use protective coatings and circular motion that follows hair growth.[1] These statements come from an AI-generated source and are not drawn from a controlled trial.

Wikipedia's article on pseudofolliculitis barbae, the razor-bump condition associated with close shaving of curly or thick hair, says some men use electric razors to prevent it, advises against too close a shave, and gives an optimal stubble length of about 0.5 to 1 mm, with a trimmer on its lowest setting as an alternative to shaving. It lists growing a beard as the most effective prevention.[9]

Wikipedia's shaving article says electric shavers cause fewer cuts and can reduce razor bumps but may not cut as closely, and that manual razors give a closer shave.[6] Grokipedia says users may need one to two weeks to adjust to the motion and vibration.[1] It also cites online discussions in which the Panasonic Arc 5 and 6 are praised for closeness, the Braun Series 9 for comfort on sensitive skin, and budget foil models from Braun and Andis as alternatives, while noting these are user opinions rather than tests.[1]

No studies found comparing electric shavers with other methods for appearance outcomes. A 2016 review summarises manufacturer-side research on skin irritation from electric shaving and on design features intended to reduce it.[7]

Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis linked to a shaver itself: one report assessed nickel release from an electric shaver in a case of allergic nickel dermatitis,[10] and another described facial contact dermatitis from fragrance ingredients released by an electric shaver.[11] These are isolated reports, not estimates of how common such reactions are.

Shaving of any kind can cause irritation, and the 2016 review treats electric-shaving irritation as an area for ongoing design improvement.[7] Wikipedia notes that for electrical safety the charging cord should be unplugged before a shaver is cleaned in water, and wet/dry models are battery powered.[2]

Electric shaving sits in the grooming category of appearance advice, alongside beard trimming and skin care. It appears in forum discussion mainly as a durability and comfort topic: a Lemmy buy-it-for-life thread about men's electric shavers drew 16 comments, and its original poster described a 16-year-old Braun foil shaver as having 'outlasted basically every other consumer electronic' they owned.[8]

For users with curly or coarse beards who get razor bumps, Wikipedia's article on pseudofolliculitis barbae mentions electric razors, trimmers on the lowest setting and beard growth as strategies, which is where shaver choice intersects with skin concerns.[9] Wikipedia also notes that shaving does not make hair grow back thicker or darker; hair can look darker because the cut end is blunt.[6]

lore.intro: Electric shavers come up in grooming and buy-it-for-life discussions, mostly as durability, closeness and sensitive-skin questions rather than as looksmaxxing techniques.[8][1]

claims.claim: Foil shavers give a closer shave than rotary shavers.
Rotary heads handle jaw and neck contours and longer growth better.
Electric shaving causes fewer ingrown hairs and razor bumps than blades.
A good shaver can last decades.
Electric shaving can cause contact allergy.
